--- title: "Retail Campaign Effectiveness" author: "Tilabo Williamson" date: "2026-10-25" editor: markdown: wrap: 72 --- ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: # 1. Background Retailers often invest in **direct-marketing campaigns**, such as coupons. Households are given coupons as part of these marketing scheme but the question is: > Do these campaigns increase household spend, and do all household > types respond in the same way? This first four sections of this project explain the data, check its quality, describe how households shop and the campaigns looked at in this analysis. Later sections will measure the effect of the campaigns themselves. Each section follows the same pattern: what we look at, what we found, and what it means for the campaign analysis. ## About the data The data covers two years of grocery shopping by 2500 households who shop regularly at one U.S. retailer. It records every product they bought, as well as which households were targeted by 30 direct-marketing campaigns and which coupons were redeemed. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Reading in the data transactions <- read_csv("data/raw/transaction_data.csv") %>% clean_names() products <- read_csv("data/raw/product.csv") %>% clean_names() demographics <- read_csv("data/raw/hh_demographic.csv") %>% clean_names() campaign_desc <- read_csv("data/raw/campaign_desc.csv") %>% clean_names() campaign_hh <- read_csv("data/raw/campaign_table.csv") %>% clean_names() redemptions <- read_csv("data/raw/coupon_redempt.csv") %>% clean_names() ``` ::: Six data sets are examined in this analysis. The transactions data set is the core of the analysis. It contains one row for every product on every receipt. The other data sets describe the products, households and campaigns, and link to it through shared IDs such as `household_key` and `product_id`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Data set summary tables_used <- tibble( Table = c("transactions", "products", "demographics", "campaign_desc", "campaign_hh", "redemptions"), `What it holds` = c( "Every product bought, one row per product per receipt", "Product details such as department and brand", "Age, income and household size (some households only)", "The 30 campaigns and their start and end days", "Which households were targeted by which campaign", "Which households redeemed a coupon, and when" ), Rows = big(c(nrow(transactions), nrow(products), nrow(demographics), nrow(campaign_desc), nrow(campaign_hh), nrow(redemptions))) ) # Display in kable tables_used %>% kable(caption = "The six data sets used in this report", align = c("l", "l", "r")) %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
The six data sets used in this report
Table What it holds Rows
transactions Every product bought, one row per product per receipt 2,595,732
products Product details such as department and brand 92,353
demographics Age, income and household size (some households only) 801
campaign_desc The 30 campaigns and their start and end days 30
campaign_hh Which households were targeted by which campaign 7,208
redemptions Which households redeemed a coupon, and when 2,318
````` ::: ::: ### Key terms - **Household:** one shopping household, identified by a household key. - **Basket:** one shopping trip. All line items bought together share the same basket ID. - **Line item:** one product on one receipt. Each row of the transactions table is a line item. - **Campaign:** a direct-marketing effort sent to chosen households, usually with coupons. ### Variables in the transactions data set The two key variable sin the `transactions` data set are `sales_value` (the money received for a line) and `quantity` (the number of units bought). Two units of a \$1.50 item is a quantity of 2 and a sales value of about \$3.00. Spend in this report is measured with sales value. Below is a table summarising key variables from the `transactions` data set. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # What each column in the transactions table means variable_dictionary <- tibble( Variable = c("household_key", "basket_id", "day", "week_no", "product_id", "store_id", "quantity", "sales_value", "retail_disc", "coupon_disc", "coupon_match_disc", "trans_time"), Meaning = c( "Unique ID for the household that shopped", "Unique ID for one shopping trip; links all items bought together", "Day of the purchase, counted from the start of the data", "Week of the purchase, counted from the start of the data", "Unique ID for the product; links to the products table", "Store where the purchase was made", "Number of units of that product bought on that line", "Money the retailer received for that line, in dollars", "Discount from the retailer's loyalty-card programme (stored as a negative number)", "Discount from a manufacturer coupon", "Discount from the retailer matching a manufacturer coupon", "Time of day of the purchase on a 24-hour clock (1631 = 4:31 pm)" ) ) # Display in kable variable_dictionary %>% kable(caption = "Variable dictionary: transactions table") %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Variable dictionary: transactions table
Variable Meaning
household_key Unique ID for the household that shopped
basket_id Unique ID for one shopping trip; links all items bought together
day Day of the purchase, counted from the start of the data
week_no Week of the purchase, counted from the start of the data
product_id Unique ID for the product; links to the products table
store_id Store where the purchase was made
quantity Number of units of that product bought on that line
sales_value Money the retailer received for that line, in dollars
retail_disc Discount from the retailer's loyalty-card programme (stored as a negative number)
coupon_disc Discount from a manufacturer coupon
coupon_match_disc Discount from the retailer matching a manufacturer coupon
trans_time Time of day of the purchase on a 24-hour clock (1631 = 4:31 pm)
````` ::: ::: # 2. Data Quality Before describing or analysing the data, it was checked that it is complete, free of duplicates and free of values that would distort the results. ## Missingness First the data was examined for missingness. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Count missing values in each column missing_wide <- transactions %>% summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) # Turn the wide row into a long table, one row per column missing_long <- missing_wide %>% pivot_longer( cols = everything(), names_to = "Column", values_to = "Missing values" ) # Display in kable missing_long %>% kable(caption = "Missing values per column in the transactions table") %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Missing values per column in the transactions table
Column Missing values
household_key 0
basket_id 0
day 0
product_id 0
quantity 0
sales_value 0
store_id 0
retail_disc 0
trans_time 0
week_no 0
coupon_disc 0
coupon_match_disc 0
````` ::: ::: Across all 12 columns of the `transactions` data set, all columns have 0 rows containing missing data. ## Duplications Next we examined the transaction data set for rows that were duplicates. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Count of any duplicate rows n_duplicates <- sum(duplicated(transactions)) cat("Number of duplicate rows:", n_duplicates, "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of duplicate rows: 0 ``` ::: ::: The `transactions` data set contained **0** duplicate rows. ## Data counts The next table shows the counts of key variables in the transaction data set. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Counts of people, baskets, products, stores, time data_counts <- transactions %>% summarise( households = n_distinct(household_key), baskets = n_distinct(basket_id), products = n_distinct(product_id), stores = n_distinct(store_id), first_day = min(day), last_day = max(day), first_week = min(week_no), last_week = max(week_no) ) # Turn the wide row into a long table, one row per column data_counts_long <- data_counts %>% pivot_longer( cols = everything(), names_to = "Column", values_to = "Data Counts" ) # Display in kable data_counts_long %>% kable(caption = "Counts of key variables from the transaction dataset") %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Counts of key variables from the transaction dataset
Column Data Counts
households 2500
baskets 276484
products 92339
stores 582
first_day 1
last_day 711
first_week 1
last_week 102
````` ::: ::: The data covers **2,500** households, **276,484** shopping trips and **92,339** different products across **582** stores. It runs for **102** weeks (711 days). ## Sales and quantity values Checks for zero or negative sales and zero quantities, which can distort spend totals.. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sales and quantity values sales_quantity_values <- transactions %>% summarise( zero_sales = sum(sales_value == 0), negative_value_sales = sum(sales_value < 0), zero_quantity = sum(quantity == 0), min_sales = min(sales_value), max_sales = max(sales_value) ) # Turn the wide row into a long table, one row per column sales_quantity_values_wide <- sales_quantity_values %>% pivot_longer( cols = everything(), names_to = "Column", values_to = "Values" ) # Display in kable sales_quantity_values_wide %>% kable(caption = "Sales and quantity values") %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Sales and quantity values
Column Values
zero_sales 18850
negative_value_sales 0
zero_quantity 14466
min_sales 0
max_sales 840
````` ::: ::: There are no negative sales values, so no returns or refunds are recorded as negative sales. However, **18,850** lines (0.73% of all lines) have a sales value of zero, and **14,466** lines (0.56%) have a quantity of zero. **What this means for the analysis:** - **Spend:** Lines with zero sales add nothing to a household's total spend, so they don't distort spend totals. - **Averages per line:** They do pull the average line value down slightly, because they count as lines. Household and basket totals are not affected. - **Units:** A quantity of zero can't be used to work out a price per unit, because dividing by zero gives an error. Quantity is not used for that in this report. - **Scale:** Both groups are under 1% of the data, so the main results are very unlikely to change. These rows are kept in, and flagged here for transparency. ## Demographic coverage Shows how many shoppers have demographic details, which limits every analysis by age, income or household size to that subset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # What share of shoppers have demographic information? households_in_transactions <- n_distinct(transactions$household_key) households_in_demographics <- n_distinct(demographics$household_key) # Households with demographic details, and the share of all households cat("Households in the transactions data:", households_in_transactions, "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Households in the transactions data: 2500 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Households with demographic details:", households_in_demographics, "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Households with demographic details: 801 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Share with demographic details:", scales::percent(households_in_demographics / households_in_transactions, accuracy = 0.1), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Share with demographic details: 32.0% ``` ::: ::: Only **801** of **2,500** households (32%) have demographic details. Any breakdown by age, income or household size describes this group only, not all shoppers. # 3. Descriptive Statistics This section describes how much households buy and how much their spending varies. In the tables, **Mean (SD)** is the average with the spread around it, and **Median** is the middle value. When a few large values pull the mean up, the median is a better picture of a typical case. ## Line-item summary Summarises the size and spread of each purchase line, which shows how skewed spending is before any grouping. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Put sales and quantity in one long column so we can summarise both at once line_item_summary <- transactions %>% select(sales_value, quantity) %>% pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>% group_by(Variable) %>% summarise( `Mean (SD)` = paste0(round(mean(Value), 2), " (", round(sd(Value), 2), ")"), Median = round(median(Value), 2), Min = min(Value), Max = max(Value) ) # Display in kable line_item_summary %>% kable(caption = "Line-item summary: sales value and quantity") %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Line-item summary: sales value and quantity
Variable Mean (SD) Median Min Max
quantity 100.43 (1153.44) 1 0 89638
sales_value 3.1 (4.18) 2 0 840
````` ::: ::: The typical line item is worth **$2.00** (median), and the average is **$3.10** (SD $4.18). The average is higher because a few expensive items pull it up. Quantity is more extreme: a few lines record very large quantities (the largest is 89,638 units). Because of this, quantity is not used in this report and spend is measured with sales value. ## Household totals Builds one row per household (total spend, number of trips, average basket value), because most later analyses compare households, not single purchases. Most of the later analysis compares households, so each household's purchases are added up into a single row. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Total sales value and number of baskets for each household household_totals <- transactions %>% group_by(household_key) %>% summarise( total_spend = sum(sales_value), trips = n_distinct(basket_id) ) %>% mutate(avg_basket_value = total_spend / trips) # average spend per trip # Show the first five households as a check household_totals %>% head(5) %>% mutate( total_spend = usd2(total_spend), avg_basket_value = usd2(avg_basket_value) ) %>% kable(caption = "First five households", col.names = c("Household", "Total spend", "Trips", "Average basket value"), align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")) %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
First five households
Household Total spend Trips Average basket value
1 $4,330.16 86 $50.35
2 $1,954.34 45 $43.43
3 $2,653.21 47 $56.45
4 $1,200.11 30 $40.00
5 $779.06 40 $19.48
````` ::: ::: - **Total spend:** everything the household spent over the two years. - **Trips:** the number of separate shopping trips (baskets). - **Average basket value:** total spend divided by trips. A typical household spent **$2,158** over the two years (median), made **79** trips and spent **$27.42** per trip. Average spend is higher, at **$3,223** (SD $3,349), and the SD is almost as large as the mean. Households vary a lot: some shop far more than others. ## Household summary Shows the typical household's spend, trips and basket size, with how much they vary, which sets the baseline for judging campaign effects. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Same summary as before, now at household level household_summary <- household_totals %>% select(total_spend, trips, avg_basket_value) %>% pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>% group_by(Variable) %>% summarise( `Mean (SD)` = paste0(round(mean(Value), 2), " (", round(sd(Value), 2), ")"), Median = round(median(Value), 2), Min = round(min(Value), 2), Max = round(max(Value), 2) ) # Display in kable household_summary %>% kable(caption = "Household summary") %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Household summary
Variable Mean (SD) Median Min Max
avg_basket_value 31.62 (19.05) 27.42 2.39 165.83
total_spend 3222.99 (3349.03) 2157.75 8.17 38319.79
trips 110.59 (115.67) 79.00 1.00 1300.00
````` ::: ::: A typical household spent **$2,158** over the two years (median), made **79** trips and spent **$27.42** per trip. Average spend is higher, at **$3,223** (SD $3,349), and the SD is almost as large as the mean. Households vary a lot, meaning some shop far more than others. ### Distribution of household spend A typical household spent **$2,158** over the two years (median). The chart shows whether most households spend a similar amount or a few spend far more. If the mean sits to the right of the median, a few heavy spenders are pulling the average up. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Summary numbers used to label the chart spend_mean <- mean(household_totals$total_spend) spend_sd <- sd(household_totals$total_spend) spend_median <- median(household_totals$total_spend) spend_min <- min(household_totals$total_spend) spend_max <- max(household_totals$total_spend) household_totals %>% ggplot(aes(x = total_spend)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = lavender, colour = "white") + geom_vline(xintercept = spend_median, colour = deeppurple, linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = spend_mean, colour = coral, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") + annotate("text", x = spend_median, y = Inf, hjust = 1.08, vjust = 1.6, label = paste0("Median: ", usd0(spend_median)), colour = deeppurple, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) + annotate("text", x = spend_mean, y = Inf, hjust = -0.08, vjust = 1.6, label = paste0("Mean: ", usd0(spend_mean), " (SD ", usd0(spend_sd), ")"), colour = coral, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.2, 0.05)),labels = usd0) + scale_y_continuous(labels = big, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) + labs( title = "Total spend per household over two years", subtitle = paste0("Range: ", usd0(spend_min), " to ", usd0(spend_max), " across ", big(nrow(household_totals)), " households"), x = "Total spend over two years", y = "Number of households", caption = "Solid line = median; dashed line = mean." ) + theme_report ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](retail-campaign-effectiveness_files/figure-html/household-spend-histogram-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Most households sit at the lower end, with a long tail of heavy spenders reaching **$38,320**. The mean (dashed line) sits to the right of the median (solid line), which confirms the skew. For the campaign analysis, this means comparing each household with itself before and during a campaign is fairer than comparing different households with each other. ### Distribution of basket value Shows how much a typical shopping trip is worth, and how skewed trip size is. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Total value of each basket (one shopping trip) basket_values <- transactions %>% group_by(basket_id) %>% summarise(basket_value = sum(sales_value)) # Summary numbers use ALL baskets basket_mean <- mean(basket_values$basket_value) basket_sd <- sd(basket_values$basket_value) basket_median <- median(basket_values$basket_value) basket_min <- min(basket_values$basket_value) basket_max <- max(basket_values$basket_value) # Cut off the top 1% of baskets in the chart only, so a few huge baskets do not squash it cutoff <- quantile(basket_values$basket_value, 0.99) basket_values %>% filter(basket_value <= cutoff) %>% ggplot(aes(x = basket_value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = lavender, colour = "white") + geom_vline(xintercept = basket_median, colour = deeppurple, linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = basket_mean, colour = coral, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") + annotate("text", x = basket_median, y = Inf, hjust = 1.08, vjust = 1.6, label = paste0("Median: ", usd2(basket_median)), colour = deeppurple, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) + annotate("text", x = basket_mean, y = Inf, hjust = -0.08, vjust = 1.6, label = paste0("Mean: ", usd2(basket_mean), " (SD ", usd2(basket_sd), ")"), colour = coral, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.2, 0.05)), labels = usd0) + scale_y_continuous(labels = big, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) + labs( title = "Value of each shopping trip", subtitle = paste0("All ", big(nrow(basket_values)), " baskets range from ", usd2(basket_min), " to ", usd2(basket_max), ". The chart hides the top 1% (above ", usd0(cutoff), ")."), x = "Basket value", y = "Number of baskets", caption = "Solid line = median; dashed line = mean. Mean, SD and range use all baskets." ) + theme_report ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](retail-campaign-effectiveness_files/figure-html/basket-value-histogram-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: A typical trip is worth **$17.07** (median), and the average is **$29.14** (SD $36.10). Most trips are modest, and a few large shops pull the average up. The chart hides the top 1% of baskets (above $174) so the main shape is visible, but the figures use every basket. ## Weekly sales over time This chart shows total sales for each week. The sharp rise at the start is not a spending boom. It happens because households enter the data gradually, which the next two charts show. Weeks 1 to 19 are shaded as a warm-up period. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Total sales for every week in the data weekly_sales <- transactions %>% group_by(week_no) %>% summarise(weekly_sales = sum(sales_value)) # Summary numbers and the best and worst weeks, used for labels weekly_mean <- mean(weekly_sales$weekly_sales) weekly_sd <- sd(weekly_sales$weekly_sales) peak_week <- weekly_sales %>% slice_max(weekly_sales, n = 1) low_week <- weekly_sales %>% slice_min(weekly_sales, n = 1) weekly_sales %>% ggplot(aes(x = week_no, y = weekly_sales)) + geom_line(colour = deeppurple, linewidth = 0.9) + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = 19.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = lavender, alpha = 0.25) + annotate("text", x = 10, y = Inf, vjust = 1.6, label = "Warm-up period\n(weeks 1 to 19)", colour = deeppurple, fontface = "bold", size = 4) + geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = coral, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(data = peak_week, colour = lavender, size = 3.5) + geom_point(data = low_week, colour = coral, size = 3.5) + geom_label(data = peak_week, vjust = -0.7, colour = lavender, fontface = "bold", aes(label = paste0("Highest: ", usd0(weekly_sales), " (week ", week_no, ")"))) + geom_label(data = low_week, vjust = 1.7, colour = coral, fontface = "bold", aes(label = paste0("Lowest: ", usd0(weekly_sales), " (week ", week_no, ")"))) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.3, 0.2)), breaks = seq(0, 104, by = 13)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = usd0, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.12, 0.15))) + labs( title = "Total sales per week", subtitle = "Sales rise sharply while households join the data, then level off", x = "Week number", y = "Total sales", caption = "Dark purple line = weekly total; dashed coral line = smoothed trend; shaded area = warm-up weeks excluded from baseline comparisons." ) + theme_report ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](retail-campaign-effectiveness_files/figure-html/weekly-sales-line-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: The next two charts split total sales into its two parts: how many households shopped each week, and how much each of them spent. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Count how many different households shopped in each week, and the sales per active household active_households <- transactions %>% group_by(week_no) %>% summarise( active_households = n_distinct(household_key), weekly_sales = sum(sales_value) ) %>% mutate(sales_per_active_household = weekly_sales / active_households) # Summary numbers used in the chart subtitles hh_mean <- mean(active_households$active_households) hh_sd <- sd(active_households$active_households) sp_mean <- mean(active_households$sales_per_active_household) sp_sd <- sd(active_households$sales_per_active_household) # Chart 1: how many households shopped each week chart_active <- active_households %>% ggplot(aes(x = week_no, y = active_households)) + geom_line(colour = deeppurple, linewidth = 0.9) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 104, by = 13)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = big, limits = c(0, NA)) + labs( title = "Households shopping each week", subtitle = paste0("Mean ", big(round(hh_mean)), " (SD ", big(round(hh_sd)), "); range ", big(min(active_households$active_households)), " to ", big(max(active_households$active_households))), x = "Week number", y = "Active households" ) + theme_report # Chart 2: sales per active household each week chart_per_household <- active_households %>% ggplot(aes(x = week_no, y = sales_per_active_household)) + geom_line(colour = coral, linewidth = 0.9) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = deeppurple) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 104, by = 13)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = usd2, limits = c(0, NA)) + labs( title = "Sales per active household each week", subtitle = paste0("Mean ", usd2(sp_mean), " (SD ", usd2(sp_sd), "); range ", usd2(min(active_households$sales_per_active_household)), " to ", usd2(max(active_households$sales_per_active_household))), x = "Week number", y = "Sales per household" ) + theme_report # Stack the two charts (patchwork is already loaded) chart_active / chart_per_household ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](retail-campaign-effectiveness_files/figure-html/weekly-active-households-and-sales-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: **Top chart:** the number of households shopping each week climbs from **88** to about **1,428** and levels off around week 17. **Bottom chart:** sales per active household stay steady at **$64.41** (SD $4.51), with only a gentle upward drift (purple line). So the early rise in total sales comes from more households appearing in the data, not from households spending more. Weeks 1 to 19 are therefore excluded when comparing spend before and during campaigns. Sales dip in the final weeks, so the last week may be only partly recorded. # 4. Campaigns Before measuring any effect, we need to know what the campaigns were: how many, what type, when they ran and how many households each one targeted. ## Campaign overview Lists each campaign with its type, timing and reach, in the order they started. Weeks are worked out from the day numbers so they match the weekly charts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Count how many different households each campaign targeted campaign_targets <- campaign_hh %>% group_by(campaign) %>% summarise(households_targeted = n_distinct(household_key)) # Join the counts to the campaign descriptions and work out weeks and length campaign_overview <- campaign_desc %>% left_join(campaign_targets, by = "campaign") %>% mutate( start_week = ceiling(start_day / 7), # day 1 to 7 is week 1 end_week = ceiling(end_day / 7), length_days = end_day - start_day + 1 ) %>% arrange(start_day) %>% select(campaign, description, start_week, end_week, length_days, households_targeted) # Display in kable campaign_overview %>% kable(caption = "The campaigns in order of start date", col.names = c("Campaign", "Type", "Start week", "End week", "Length (days)", "Households targeted"), align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r")) %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ## Campaign types The campaigns come in three types, labelled A, B and C. They differ in how coupons were given out: - **Type A:** each household in the campaign received 16 coupons, chosen from a pool of coupons according to what that household had bought before. - **Type B and Type C:** every household in the campaign received all of the coupons for that campaign. This matters for the analysis. Type A coupons were matched to each household's past buying, so households may already have been likely to buy those products. Results are therefore compared by campaign type as well as overall. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Summarise the campaigns by type: how many, how long, how many households targeted campaign_types <- campaign_overview %>% group_by(description) %>% summarise( Campaigns = n(), `Length in days, mean (SD)` = paste0(round(mean(length_days)), " (", round(sd(length_days)), ")"), `Households targeted, mean (SD)` = paste0(big(round(mean(households_targeted))), " (", big(round(sd(households_targeted))), ")") ) # Display in kable campaign_types %>% kable(caption = "Campaigns by type", col.names = c("Type", "Campaigns", "Length in days, mean (SD)", "Households targeted, mean (SD)"), align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")) %>% style_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

The highest average reach was for **TypeA** campaigns, targeting an average of **796** households (SD 411). ## Campaign timeline Shows when each campaign ran against the warm-up period, so any campaign that overlaps it stands out. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Order the campaigns by start date (earliest at the top) campaign_timeline <- campaign_overview %>% mutate(campaign_label = factor(campaign, levels = rev(campaign))) campaign_timeline %>% ggplot(aes(y = campaign_label)) + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = 19.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = lavender, alpha = 0.25) + geom_segment(aes(x = start_week, xend = end_week, yend = campaign_label, colour = description), linewidth = 4) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(deeppurple, coral, lavender, purple)) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 104, by = 13)) + labs( title = "When each campaign ran", subtitle = paste0(nrow(campaign_overview), " campaigns; shaded area = warm-up weeks 1 to 19"), x = "Week number", y = "Campaign", colour = "Campaign type" ) + theme_report + theme(legend.position = "top") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](retail-campaign-effectiveness_files/figure-html/campaign-timeline-1.png){width=960} ::: :::
